overview: This card covers the modern Kyrgyz Republic, whose independence declaration was adopted on 31 August 1991. The atlas begins only in 1994 and repeats one simplified polygon for three intervals ending in 2020, although the state continues. Bishkek, Osh, Naryn, Karakol and Batken fall inside the tested outline; Almaty, Tashkent and Kashgar do not. It is a map layer, not a legal border survey.

periods.title: Independence and the Akaev presidency
periods.summary: The republic separated from the Soviet Union and built new institutions under President Askar Akaev.

periods.title: The 2005 uprising and Bakiyev government
periods.summary: Mass protest forced Akaev to resign; Kurmanbek Bakiyev then held the presidency until another upheaval.

periods.title: Parliamentary-era constitution
periods.summary: A 2010 constitutional settlement reduced presidential power, and the 2017 vote produced an orderly elected succession.

periods.title: Annulled vote and rapid transition
periods.summary: The October parliamentary result was annulled after fraud claims; an early presidential election and system referendum followed.

periods.title: Renewed presidential system
periods.summary: The 2021 Constitution strengthened the presidency; Sadyr Japarov was serving as president in September 2026, after observers found the 2025 parliamentary campaign increasingly restrictive.

sections.title: Independence, repeated political change and written Kyrgyz

items.text: The Supreme Soviet adopted the declaration of state independence on 31 August 1991. That event predates this atlas record by three years. Kyrgyz societies, languages and landscapes are much older, while the modern republic is the sovereign institution founded in 1991.

Public pressure changed governments twice in five years. Askar Akaev resigned after the March 2005 protests. On 7 April 2010 another revolution removed Kurmanbek Bakiyev, and an interim government led by Roza Otunbayeva prepared a new constitutional order. These turnovers were political changes within the same continuing republic.

The October 2017 election mattered because it enabled a transfer from one elected president to another. International observers called the contest competitive, while also recording pressure on voters, vote buying, misuse of public resources and problems during counting. A peaceful handover and serious election flaws can both be part of the same assessment.

After the 2020 parliamentary vote was annulled, voters faced an early presidential election and a referendum on the form of government on the same day in January 2021. ODIHR said the process was organized well but one candidate dominated resources and visibility, and linking the contests weakened public debate. The later Constitution restored a strongly presidential system.

A modern Kyrgyz sample is Кыргыз Республикасы (Кыргызстан) - көз карандысыз, эгемен, демократиялык, унитардык, укуктук, светтик жана социалдык мамлекет. It means “The Kyrgyz Republic (Kyrgyzstan) is an independent, sovereign, democratic, unitary, law-based, secular and social state.” The official Constitution prints this in Cyrillic; letters such as ы, ө and ү help show that this is Kyrgyz, not Russian.

sections.title: Growth, public projects and much older places

items.text: The World Bank reports that real output grew 11.1 per cent in 2025, driven by consumption, investment, services, construction and industry. It also reports 8.2 per cent average inflation and continued exposure to gold prices, remittances and outside shocks. Fast national growth can coexist with dearer groceries and uneven household gains.

Sulaiman-Too above Osh was sacred for at least fifteen centuries before the modern republic. Its paths link petroglyphs, caves, worship places and reconstructed mosques at a Silk Roads crossroads. Kyrgyzstan now helps protect this inherited landscape, but UNESCO warns that construction around the mountain can damage its setting. The republic is its steward, not its ancient builder.

Communities began coordinating the revival of traditional games after independence, and Kyrgyzstan hosted the first World Nomad Games in 2014. UNESCO treats the programme as a way to exchange knowledge and safeguard varied traditions. It was not a time machine and it did not make every nomadic game Kyrgyz; it created a modern meeting place for many communities.

World Bank reporting describes literacy as universal and places Kyrgyzstan's human-capital measures high among countries at similar income levels. Those broad indicators are achievements, but they do not erase differences in school access, learning quality or income. A national average is a useful dashboard light, not a photograph of every child.

sections.title: Felt, family memory and a hat with four sides

items.text: Ala-kiyiz and shyrdak carpets traditionally warmed and decorated homes. UNESCO describes groups working together and older women passing skills to younger women in families. It also lists shrinking practitioner numbers, synthetic carpets and scarce raw material as threats. The floor can be art, insulation and a family lesson all at once, but the lesson survives only if somebody has time to teach it.

A yurt has a collapsible circular wooden frame, felt covering and ropes, so experienced makers can take it apart and move it. UNESCO documents men making frames and women making coverings in the practising communities, with skills passed through families and apprenticeships. Some yurts accompany births, weddings and funerals and are handed down as family relics. It is a house that can travel, while family memories ride along.

The ak-kalpak is a white felt men's hat with more than eighty documented forms. Makers felt, cut, sew and embroider it, teaching by talking, demonstrating and working side by side. Community explanations compare its shape to a snowy peak and connect its four sides with four elements. In other words, it can keep a head covered while carrying a small mountain of symbolism.

sections.title: School, medicine and toilets that children can actually use

items.text: A three-year catch-up programme after pandemic closures supplied more than 1,000 computers and trained over 10,300 teachers. UNICEF reported support for 20,500 pupils in Grades 5 and 6 and test-score gains of 15 to 20 percentage points among participants. These measured programme results are encouraging, though they do not describe every pupil in Kyrgyzstan.

In one Chuy village, three-year-old Altynai attends an early-learning centre inside a public library. Her centre opened in late 2024 for 26 children, and UNICEF reported 300 such library centres nationwide. A room once expected to whisper can now contain storybooks, exercises and preschool giggles. The project expands options, while poorer and rural families still face larger access gaps.

Nurse Jiydegul Rysbaeva has ridden horseback across the Jon-Bulak Valley for more than 36 years to bring vaccines and care to children on 41 remote farmsteads. She also talks with hesitant parents. The route can include howling wolves, which makes “the clinic is a long ride away” unusually literal. Her work shows both dedication and the difficulty of mountain access.

UNICEF says about one household in five is connected to centralized sewerage, while most people rely on onsite systems such as septic pits. Rural schools often lack indoor toilets, hot water, privacy and safe facilities for girls; sinks may sit inconveniently far from latrines. Work on affordable local toilet designs matters because a toilet across a cold yard is technically present but can still be practically unusable.

ending.text: Kyrgyzstan remains a continuing state. The atlas stopping its last polygon interval in 2020 does not mark an ending. As of September 2026, Sadyr Japarov was president under the system established in 2021; ODIHR's assessment of the November 2025 parliamentary election found efficient administration alongside a restrictive campaign and shrinking practical freedoms. Political institutions may change again while families, communities and public services follow their own longer histories.
